subject: Obtaining yearly predictions from fitted values

messages.author: 99551dc1e4502c1d
messages.subject: Obtaining yearly predictions from fitted values
parts:
Hi

I am running a joint hurdle model looking at the occurrence of a fish species. I am trying to get yearly occurrence predictions using summary.fitted.values by referencing my prediction stack (with y=NA) however I'm not sure the code is correct. I am predicting to each mesh node and so call 1:n_mesh_nodes when running inla.mesh.project, this seems to work fine for year 1 but when I try to get predictions for the following year they are either the exact same, or make no sense. I was able to join a set of covariates to each mesh node using the nearest neighbour function and so obtain my new locations for predicting to (which matched the number of mesh nodes). 

Example, with 400 mesh nodes I would use:

## get predictions for the prediction stack
index_pred <- inla.stack.index(joint.stack,"pred")$data
lp_sum<-test$summary.fitted.values$mean[index_pred]

## select the first n rows of predictions to match number of mesh nodes
lp_sum1<-as.data.frame(lp_sum)
lp_sum1= lp_sum1[1:400,]

u.proj<-inla.mesh.projector(q_mesh1)
m.proj<-inla.mesh.project(u.proj, lp_sum1) 


and for the following year use lp_sum1= lp_sum1[401:800,]

Is this the correct way to obtain yearly predictions? Sample code and files attached.

Any help is greatly appreciated!

Thanks,

Paul

messages.author: 9940b4fcc153c7d7
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Obtaining yearly predictions from fitted values
parts:
Hi Paul,

To check your code in general, I suggest making up some known space-time surface, adding noise and seeing if you can recover said surface. Very small noise with fixed (known) variance (control.family=...).

Predicting to each mesh node depends on the structure of your formula. The space-time effects can be predicted by just extracting it at the mesh nodes in space-time, as you would do when plotting (before projection to a grid). The other effects in the predictor depend on how you want to interpolate them to the mesh nodes.

If you have all the space-time covariate information at the space-time mesh nodes, the NA trick you are doing might work. To do this you need NA for each mesh node at each time point! However, the NA trick in the space-time models have some stability issues, because you are adding #meshnodes*#years fake datapoints, and constructing the predictor based on posterior samples of each random and fixed effect may be safer.

To check that the $time covariate in the stack comes in the order you think that it does, you can do "(str(stack))" and investigate the object

You can also make two separate stacks for the first 2 years to be sure of the indexing, and compare it to what you are doing now. You can even fit two different models with the two different years' prediction stacks (using the same data fitting stack in each).

PS: I checked your code briefly, and nothing stood out to me as wrong.

Kind regards,
Haakon Bakka
